title: Job Order on a Single Core
statement:
A processor with one core receives n jobs. Job i is tasks[i] = [arrive, length]: it becomes available at time arrive and needs length units of time once started. A job runs to completion without interruption.

The scheduler follows these rules:

  • When the core is free and some jobs are available, it starts the one with the shortest length; ties go to the smallest index.
  • When the core is free and nothing is available, it waits until the next job arrives.
  • Finishing one job and starting the next happen at the same instant, so a job arriving exactly when another finishes is available for that choice.

Return the indices of the jobs in the order the core runs them.

examples.why: At time 1 only job 0 is there, so it runs even though shorter jobs arrive soon after. At time 5 jobs 1 and 2 wait; job 2 is shorter. The core then idles until job 3 arrives at 10.
At time 4 jobs 0 and 3 both have length 2. Job 0 arrived later but has the smaller index, and index breaks ties, not arrival time.
The input is not in arrival order. Job 1 arrives first and finishes long before job 0 shows up.

hints: Simulate the clock. At each decision point you need the set of jobs that have arrived, and from it the shortest one. Which structure gives you that quickly?
Sort job indices by arrival time. Keep a pointer into that order and push every job with arrive ≤ now into a min-heap keyed by (length, index).
If the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next arrival instead of stepping one unit at a time. Otherwise pop the top job, record it, and add its length to the clock.

explain.intuition:
This is an event simulation. The only moments that matter are when the core becomes free. At such a moment, every job with arrive ≤ now is a candidate, and the scheduler wants the smallest (length, index). A min-heap holds exactly that set: jobs go in as they arrive, and the best one comes out on top.

To feed the heap in time order, sort the indices by arrival once and move a pointer through them. When the heap is empty the core is idle, so jump the clock straight to the next arrival; stepping one unit at a time would be hopeless with times up to 10⁹. It is the same shape as a browser's task queue picking the next ready job.
steps: Sort job indices by arrival time. Set now = 0, pointer p = 0, and an empty min-heap keyed by (length, index).
Repeat until every job is placed: if the heap is empty and now is before the next arrival, set now to that arrival.
Push every job with arrive ≤ now onto the heap and advance p.
Pop the top job, append its index to the answer, and add its length to now.
pitfalls: Breaking ties by arrival time instead of by index, as the second example shows.
Only pushing jobs that arrive strictly before now. A job arriving exactly at the finish time is a candidate.
Using 32-bit integers for the clock: it can reach about 10¹⁴.

solutions.title: Scan all waiting jobs at each step
solutions.idea: At every decision point, look through all jobs not yet run and pick the shortest available one; if none is available, jump to the earliest arrival.

solutions.title: Sort by arrival + min-heap
solutions.idea: Feed jobs into a heap keyed by (length, index) as the clock passes their arrival; jump the clock forward when the core would be idle.

followups: The core can pause a job when a shorter one arrives (preemption). How does the simulation change?
There are k identical cores. What second heap do you need?
